paragraphs: Continuous Time Bayesian Networks describe systems whose interacting components change at irregular times. Their usual formulation makes waiting times exponential, imposing a memoryless structure: how long a component has already remained in a state does not affect its remaining waiting time. This restriction helps computation but narrows the timing behavior the model can represent.

The paper replaces that restriction with arbitrary survival-time distributions by giving each node its own clock. These clocks support a collection of interacting semi-Markov chains, allowing elapsed time to influence transitions while retaining a graph that describes dependencies. Unlike extensions that introduce auxiliary states, this construction represents timing information directly through the clocks.

The authors provide algorithms for learning both model parameters and graph structure, using local dependencies to organize inference. Experiments use synthetic data and data generated by a gene regulatory network benchmark tool. The reported advantages concern extending the timing flexibility of these structured models while avoiding the tractability difficulties associated with auxiliary-state approaches.
icml-2020-continuous-time-bayesian-netwo.tldr: Node-wise clocks let continuous-time Bayesian networks represent arbitrary waiting-time distributions without introducing auxiliary states.

paragraphs: The paper studies a group of agents learning which options produce the best rewards while sharing information over a network. Communication takes time, and rewards have heavy tails, making unusually large observations an important estimation challenge. The agents must therefore coordinate exploration while dealing with both delayed information and unreliable behavior of ordinary averages.

Existing approaches use running consensus, a communication protocol built around averaging, to construct confidence intervals. The authors explain that this mechanism does not readily support robust estimation in heavy-tailed settings. Their decentralized algorithm, MP-UCB, instead combines robust reward estimation with a message-passing protocol, connecting the statistical estimator to a different way of sharing observations.

The authors prove optimal regret bounds in several problem settings and report superiority over existing methods. They also establish lower bounds for cooperative bandits, providing a reference for what algorithms can achieve, and develop efficient methods for robust location estimation. The optimality claims apply to the analyzed settings, rather than every possible communication network or reward model.
icml-2020-cooperative-multi-agent-bandit.tldr: MP-UCB combines robust estimation with decentralized message passing to achieve optimal regret in several cooperative heavy-tailed bandit settings.

paragraphs: Many prediction systems supply inputs to a later optimization problem. Predicted travel times, for example, help determine a shortest path. In this setting, prediction errors matter through the decisions they cause: reducing numerical error alone need not produce the best decision. The paper trains decision trees with this downstream purpose explicitly in view.

Its method, SPO Trees or SPOTs, uses Smart Predict-then-Optimize loss, which measures the suboptimality of decisions made using predicted parameters. The authors propose a tractable way to train trees under this objective. The resulting tree also provides an interpretable grouping of contextual features into regions associated with distinct optimal decisions.

Experiments cover synthetic and real data, including travel-time prediction for routing and click-probability prediction for news recommendation. On these datasets, SPOTs produce better decisions with substantially lower model complexity than approaches such as CART trained to minimize prediction error. The findings support aligning tree training with the quality of the eventual optimization decision while preserving an understandable decision structure.
icml-2020-decision-trees-for-decision-ma.tldr: SPO Trees train interpretable decision trees to improve downstream optimization decisions rather than merely reduce prediction error.

paragraphs: Quantizing a neural network reduces its numerical precision to lower memory use and computation, but preserving accuracy is a central challenge. This paper uses the intermediate features of a pretrained full-precision network as teaching signals. Those internal representations provide guidance for training quantized components, rather than relying only on the network's final output.

Divide and Conquer Quantization, or DCQ, divides the teacher network into sections and trains a team of quantized student sections independently. Each student learns from the intermediate features exposed by the corresponding part of the teacher. The trained sections are then joined together. Because sections can train in isolation, the approach also enables parallel training.

Across the networks studied, DCQ reports average performance improvements over DoReFa-Net of 21.6% for binary quantization and 9.3% for ternary quantization. The abstract does not characterize these as percentage-point gains. The authors also report improved accuracies when adding DCQ to existing quantized training methods, supporting intermediate-feature distillation as a useful component of quantized training.
icml-2020-divide-and-conquer-leveraging-.tldr: DCQ independently trains quantized network sections using a full-precision teacher's intermediate features, improving reported accuracy and enabling parallel training.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks aim to represent uncertainty, but scaling them can introduce underfitting and inefficient parameter use. Deep ensembles offer another route to uncertainty estimation, yet maintaining multiple models also costs resources. This paper seeks to combine advantages of these approaches through a more economical representation of uncertainty in network weights.

The proposed parameterization places a distribution on a rank-1 subspace associated with each weight matrix. The authors also use mixture approximate posteriors to represent multiple modes, allowing the uncertainty model to cover different parameter configurations. This construction makes mixtures comparatively inexpensive: the abstract reports only a 0.4% memory increase for a ResNet-50 mixture with ten components.

A systematic empirical study examines priors, variational posteriors, and training improvements. Evaluations include image models on ImageNet and CIFAR-10/100 and a recurrent model on MIMIC-III. The authors report state-of-the-art log-likelihood, accuracy, and calibration across the studied test sets and out-of-distribution variants, supporting the practical value of this restricted but efficient uncertainty parameterization.
icml-2020-efficient-and-scalable-bayesia.tldr: Rank-1 weight uncertainty and inexpensive posterior mixtures make Bayesian neural networks more scalable while delivering strong reported predictive and calibration results.

paragraphs: The paper learns representations of three-dimensional scenes directly from images, without requiring 3D supervision. Its central question is how to give an internal representation meaningful spatial structure when training does not supply that structure explicitly. The proposed answer is to constrain how the representation changes when a 3D transformation is applied.

The authors introduce a loss that enforces equivariance: the learned scene representation should transform consistently with a real three-dimensional scene. This makes transformation behavior a source of structural guidance. The formulation supports both inferring a scene representation and rendering it in real time, with results reported as comparable to models that require minutes for inference.

The work also introduces two challenging datasets containing scenes with complex lighting and backgrounds. Experiments on these datasets and standard ShapeNet benchmarks produce results the authors describe as compelling. Together, the method and evaluations suggest that enforcing appropriate transformation behavior can support useful scene representations while substantially reducing inference time in the comparisons reported.
icml-2020-equivariant-neural-rendering-1.tldr: Enforcing 3D transformation consistency lets a neural model learn scene representations from images and infer and render scenes in real time.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a value function that scores a transition between two states. Q(s, s′) measures the utility of moving from the current state to a neighboring state and then behaving optimally afterward. The representation places the value on the state transition, separating the question of which outcome is desirable from the actions used to reach it.

To derive an optimal policy, the authors develop a forward dynamics model that learns next-state predictions chosen to maximize this value. The overall formulation still supports off-policy learning, so learning can use observations generated by behavior other than the policy being developed. This connects transition evaluation with a model that seeks valuable subsequent states.

The paper highlights benefits for transferring value functions, handling redundant action spaces, and learning from state observations produced by suboptimal or completely random policies. These applications share a motivation: useful information about transitions need not be tied directly to a particular action representation or to expert-quality behavior. The stated contribution is a way to exploit that separation within off-policy learning.
icml-2020-estimating-q-s-s-with-deep-det.tldr: A state-to-state value function separates values from actions and supports off-policy learning through a model that predicts valuable next states.

paragraphs: An expert's decisions can be observable even when the model behind them is inaccessible. This paper asks how to infer the parameters of a decision model that balances multiple objectives using only a collection of observed expert choices. Portfolio management motivates the setting, where obtaining an expert's intrinsic decision-making model may be difficult.

The authors formulate this unsupervised task as inverse multiobjective optimization. The direction of inference runs from decisions back to the model parameters that could explain them. They propose a model with statistical guarantees and identify connections to K-means clustering and manifold learning, linking the decision-inference problem to methods for organizing the structure of observed data.

Those connections lead to two algorithms that solve the inverse problem through clustering and manifold learning. Numerical results support both the effectiveness of the proposed model and the computational efficiency of the algorithms. The contribution therefore combines a statistically grounded formulation with practical solution methods, making observed expert behavior a source of information about a multiobjective decision process.
icml-2020-expert-learning-through-genera.tldr: The paper infers multiobjective decision-model parameters from expert choices using statistically grounded inverse optimization and connections to clustering and manifold learning.

paragraphs: Understanding performance on unseen data becomes difficult when models have many parameters and learning involves nonconvex optimization. This paper develops a framework for studying that question in generalized linear models, described here as single-layer neural networks. It characterizes asymptotic generalization error and accommodates arbitrary nonlinearities, covering both regression and classification problems.

The framework connects generalization to several choices that are often studied separately. These include the degree of overparameterization, the model's nonlinearity, the loss function, initialization, and regularization. It also permits analysis when training and test distributions differ. This makes it possible to examine how modeling choices, learning choices, and distribution mismatch affect prediction within a common analytical setting.

The authors work through linear and logistic regression as examples. They also give a rigorous analytical explanation of double descent in generalized linear models, addressing how generalization can behave nonmonotonically as model size changes. The scope is an asymptotic theory for these single-layer models; its stated results do not establish a corresponding characterization for arbitrary deep networks.
icml-2020-generalization-error-of-genera.tldr: An asymptotic framework characterizes generalization in generalized linear models and rigorously explains their double-descent behavior.

paragraphs: The paper questions whether improving fairness must reduce classification accuracy. Its approach distinguishes the distributions a classifier ideally should distinguish from the possibly biased distributions represented by available data. This becomes a mismatched hypothesis-testing problem: evaluation against the observed data may tell a different story from evaluation against an ideal target.

Using Chernoff information, the authors prove that there always exist ideal distributions for which optimal fairness and accuracy can be achieved together. Crucially, this is an existence result about ideal distributions. The same classifier can exhibit no trade-off relative to those distributions while exhibiting a trade-off when accuracy is measured against the supplied biased dataset.

The authors also formulate an optimization problem for finding ideal distributions and derive limits explaining trade-offs on biased data. They identify conditions under which active data collection can alleviate the trade-off in practice. Their argument makes the evaluation distribution central: an apparent conflict between fairness and accuracy can depend on what the accuracy measure treats as the correct target.
icml-2020-is-there-a-trade-off-between-f.tldr: Fairness–accuracy trade-offs can depend on the evaluation distribution, with ideal distributions existing where both objectives are simultaneously optimal.

paragraphs: The paper studies agents that make context-dependent decisions while exchanging information over a network with delays. Each agent has its own decision problem, but cooperation can help the group learn. Rewards are modeled as linear functions of contexts after a kernel maps them into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, giving the formulation flexibility beyond linear functions of the original inputs.

The proposed algorithm, Coop-KernelUCB, aims to make that cooperation effective without excessive computation or communication. The authors establish near-optimal regret bounds for each agent. They also give variants with optimal per-agent regret for special cases, separating the general guarantee from stronger results available under particular cooperative problem structures.

The algorithm generalizes several existing multi-agent bandit results, placing them within a broader kernel-based treatment. Experiments use both synthetic and real-world multi-agent network benchmarks, where the authors report significant improvements over existing benchmarks. The theoretical and empirical contributions jointly address how agents can share useful information while still solving distinct contextual decision problems under delayed communication.
icml-2020-kernel-methods-for-cooperative.tldr: Coop-KernelUCB enables efficient cooperation in kernelized contextual bandits with near-optimal per-agent regret and optimal guarantees in special cases.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a target policy would perform using data collected previously under other behavior. This paper studies the statistical accuracy of that task with linear function approximation and a fixed batch of reinforcement-learning data. It analyzes regression-based fitted Q-iteration, connecting a practical evaluation procedure to the information available in the dataset.

The authors show that this procedure is equivalent to a model-based method estimating a conditional mean embedding of the transition operator. They derive a finite-sample error upper bound and a nearly matching minimax lower bound. Together, these results establish that the method's estimation error is nearly as small as the statistical limits permit in the studied setting.

A restricted chi-squared divergence captures the mismatch between the target policy's long-term distribution and the distribution of historical data. Its restriction to the function class makes the difficulty depend on both the particular problem and the chosen representation. The paper also provides a computable confidence bound that may support optimistic planning and safe policy improvement.
icml-2020-minimax-optimal-off-policy-eva.tldr: Fitted Q-iteration achieves nearly minimal off-policy evaluation error, governed by distribution mismatch measured through the chosen function class.

paragraphs: A regression model often returns one predicted outcome, but many applications also need information about uncertainty. NGBoost predicts an entire conditional probability distribution instead. This lets the model express a range of possible outcomes given the input features, which motivates its use in settings such as healthcare and weather forecasting.

The method extends gradient boosting by treating the parameters of that distribution as multiple prediction targets. Training must therefore coordinate updates to several parameters that jointly determine one predictive distribution. The authors show that the natural gradient is required to correct the training dynamics of their multiparameter boosting approach, making it a central part of the algorithm.

NGBoost supports any base learner, any distribution family with continuous parameters, and any scoring rule. This flexibility separates choices about the prediction model, uncertainty distribution, and training objective. The authors report performance matching or exceeding existing probabilistic prediction methods, alongside benefits in scalability and usability. The result is a general boosting framework for learning uncertainty-bearing predictions rather than only point estimates.
icml-2020-ngboost-natural-gradient-boost.tldr: NGBoost uses natural-gradient updates to extend boosting from point predictions to flexible conditional probability distributions.

paragraphs: Some stochastic models can generate synthetic observations even though computing the probability of an observed dataset is intractable. Likelihood-free inference uses this simulation capability to infer model parameters. The paper examines two popular approaches to this problem and asks how their apparently different training procedures fit into a shared statistical picture.

One approach trains a classifier to distinguish parameter–observation pairs produced by the simulator from pairs drawn from a reference distribution. This implicitly estimates a density ratio proportional to the likelihood. Another approach directly fits a conditional distribution over parameters given observations, including a variant that supports flexible neural density estimators for representing the posterior.

The authors show that both approaches belong to a general contrastive learning scheme. Their contribution is a unifying account that clarifies how the methods should be run and compared. This matters because classification-based ratio estimation and direct posterior estimation can then be understood through related learning principles, making their relationship explicit within the simulator-based inference setting.
icml-2020-on-contrastive-learning-for-li.tldr: A general contrastive learning framework unifies classifier-based likelihood-ratio estimation and direct posterior estimation for simulator-based inference.

paragraphs: A Boolean satisfiability solver searches for variable assignments that satisfy a formula. Its starting choices include which variables to consider first and which truth values to try. This paper addresses that initialization problem, aiming to reduce runtime by choosing an initial variable ordering and polarity based on the formula's clauses.

The proposed heuristic uses Bayesian Moment Matching. At the beginning of a run, it analyzes the clauses to compute a posterior probability distribution over variable assignments. The solver then uses this distribution to initialize its search. The contribution is therefore a probabilistic method for guiding the starting search configuration within existing SAT solvers.

Experiments compare the heuristic with random, survey propagation, Jeroslow-Wang, and default initialization across several solvers. BMM-based solvers outperform the other initialization methods on the cryptographic benchmark. On the SAT competition application benchmark, BMM-based MapleCOMSPS solves 12 additional instances and has better average runtime than its alternatives. These findings demonstrate measured gains from changing initialization in the evaluated solver and benchmark combinations.
icml-2020-online-bayesian-moment-matchin.tldr: Bayesian Moment Matching uses a SAT formula's clauses to choose better search initialization, improving results on the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper considers a seller repeatedly offering goods at posted prices to one strategic buyer. Each good has a d-dimensional feature vector, and the buyer's private valuation is a fixed function of those features. Because the buyer seeks to maximize cumulative discounted surplus, learning must account for behavior shaped by future opportunities as well as the current offer.

The seller is not assumed to know a parametric model for the valuation function. The authors introduce a nonparametric algorithm that also does not require knowing the interaction horizon in advance. To support it, they extend value-localization techniques from repeated auctions without context to the setting where valuations vary with the goods' features.

The algorithm has a tight strategic regret bound of order T raised to d/(d+1). This quantifies how cumulative regret scales with the number of interactions and the context dimension. For fixed positive dimension, the exponent is below one but increases with dimension. The result establishes an optimal scaling in the studied strategic, contextual, nonparametric setting.
icml-2020-optimal-non-parametric-learnin.tldr: A horizon-independent nonparametric pricing algorithm achieves tight strategic regret for repeated contextual sales to a single strategic buyer.

paragraphs: Normalization layers are widely used to improve neural-network training speed and generalization, yet much optimization theory studies networks without them. This paper addresses that mismatch by analyzing a two-layer network with ReLU activations and Weight Normalization. The focus is on how normalization affects the mathematical behavior of training.

The authors provide a global convergence result for this normalized nonlinear network setting. Their analysis examines how adding normalization changes the optimization landscape, connecting a practical architectural choice to the trajectories and convergence of training. Weight Normalization is the specific normalization mechanism covered by the result, rather than every normalization layer mentioned as motivation.

The analysis also shows that normalization can enable faster convergence than an unnormalized network in some settings. That qualification matters: the abstract does not claim that normalization always accelerates training. The contribution supplies theoretical support for a particular normalized architecture and identifies circumstances where the altered landscape helps optimization, narrowing the gap between common training practice and the settings typically treated by theory.
icml-2020-optimization-theory-for-relu-n.tldr: The paper proves global convergence for two-layer ReLU networks with Weight Normalization and shows faster convergence in some settings.

paragraphs: The paper studies maximization with diminishing returns under a cardinality constraint. The objective is nonmonotone, so increasing a choice can sometimes reduce its value. The goal is to obtain a strong approximate solution while reducing the number of sequentially dependent rounds, allowing function evaluations within a round to run in parallel.

For accuracy parameter epsilon, the proposed algorithm guarantees an approximation of 1/e minus epsilon. It uses O(log n log(1/epsilon) / epsilon cubed) parallel evaluation rounds. The approximation nearly matches the best known sequential guarantee, while the round count is nearly optimal for constant epsilon. Previous parallel algorithms have weaker guarantees and require at least order log-squared n rounds.

Experiments suggest that the resulting objective values nearly match those of leading sequential algorithms. The method also outperforms previous parallel algorithms in rounds, iterations, and solution quality in the reported evaluation. The contribution combines a theoretical approximation guarantee with reduced sequential dependence; the empirical near-match to sequential solution quality remains an experimental finding.
icml-2020-parallel-algorithm-for-non-mon.tldr: A parallel algorithm nearly matches the best known sequential approximation guarantee for nonmonotone diminishing-returns maximization using nearly optimal rounds.

paragraphs: The paper studies a seller choosing reserve prices across repeated second-price auctions with multiple strategic bidders. Each bidder has a fixed private valuation and seeks to maximize expected cumulative discounted surplus. The seller must learn useful pricing information while accounting for bidders whose decisions reflect their anticipated future gains.

The proposed method builds on a transformation that turns an algorithm for a single-buyer setting into one for multiple buyers. This is consequential because rivals create uncertainty about a bidder's future opportunities. The authors provide theoretical guarantees that a transformed algorithm can still learn a strategic buyer's valuation in the presence of that uncertainty.

Using this construction, the paper introduces a pricing algorithm with a strategic regret upper bound of O(log log T), even for worst-case valuations. The bound gives a very slowly growing guarantee on cumulative regret as the number of auctions increases. Its setting retains the stated fixed-valuation and discounted-surplus assumptions, so the result concerns this particular repeated strategic auction model.
icml-2020-reserve-pricing-in-repeated-se.tldr: A transformation from single-buyer learning yields reserve pricing with O(log log T) strategic regret for repeated auctions with multiple fixed-valuation bidders.

paragraphs: Convolutional layers apply shared filters across spatial positions, encoding an assumption that similar visual patterns should be processed similarly wherever they occur. Fully locally connected layers remove that sharing but often perform poorly. This paper investigates whether a controlled amount of position dependence can work better than either of these choices.

The authors construct a low-rank locally connected layer. At each location, its filter bank is a linear combination of shared basis filter banks, with combination weights that vary spatially. Changing the number of basis banks controls how much the layer can relax spatial invariance. This supplies a way to vary the architectural assumption rather than simply keep or discard it.

Experiments with small convolutional networks find improved classification accuracy over both convolutional and locally connected layers on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CelebA. The results suggest that strict spatial invariance can be overly restrictive in these settings. They support the value of an intermediate degree of sharing without establishing that the same relaxation is preferable for every architecture or task.
icml-2020-revisiting-spatial-invariance-.tldr: Low-rank locally connected layers relax spatial filter sharing in a controlled way and improve accuracy in experiments with small convolutional networks.

paragraphs: Frank-Wolfe methods solve constrained optimization problems using linear minimization instead of projection. This can be useful when linear minimization is cheaper or when sparse solutions need to be preserved. However, losses in applications such as Poisson inverse problems and quantum state tomography can have unbounded curvature, leaving existing Frank-Wolfe guarantees inapplicable.

The paper uses the structure of self-concordant functions to analyze these difficult losses. It introduces an adaptive step size and proves a global convergence rate of O(1/k) after k iterations. The step-size rule connects the optimization procedure to properties of the objective that remain useful when a conventional bounded-curvature analysis is unavailable.

A second method achieves linear convergence for self-concordant objectives if the problem provides a stronger local linear minimization oracle. The stronger rate is therefore conditional on access to that additional capability. Together, the results extend convergence theory for projection-free optimization and show how the available oracle determines which convergence guarantee the method can support.
icml-2020-self-concordant-analysis-of-fr.tldr: Self-concordant analysis yields convergent Frank-Wolfe methods for unbounded-curvature losses, with linear convergence when a stronger local oracle is available.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process inference can become expensive when it requires operations on large covariance matrices. This paper proposes a class of inter-domain variational Gaussian processes that first maps data onto a unit hypersphere. The construction then uses spherical harmonics to represent features, changing the representation used to make approximate inference computationally manageable.

A central benefit is that the covariance matrix between inducing variables becomes diagonal. This avoids the need to invert a large covariance matrix and enables faster inference. The authors compare the scheme conceptually with variational Fourier features and state that their approach avoids the curse of dimensionality affecting that alternative.

In a regression experiment with six million entries, the method fits the model two orders of magnitude faster than standard sparse Gaussian processes while retaining state-of-the-art accuracy. The authors also report competitive classification performance with non-conjugate likelihoods. These findings connect the computational advantage of the inducing-variable structure to substantial measured speed gains and useful predictive performance in the studied tasks.
icml-2020-sparse-gaussian-processes-with.tldr: Spherical harmonic features produce diagonal inducing-variable covariances, enabling substantially faster sparse Gaussian-process inference in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Predicting where a hospital patient will be admitted can help with limited resources and available space, particularly for patients arriving through an emergency department. This paper approaches the prediction task through curriculum learning: a teacher network learns which training data a student network should receive as the student's training progresses.

The teacher uses reinforcement learning. Its input state is a representation of the student's weights, giving it information about the model it is teaching. Its action selects a batch from a training set ordered by entropy. The curriculum is therefore a learned sequence of training selections informed by the student's evolving state.

Evaluation on three datasets shows better performance than state-of-the-art methods on tabular data and competitive performance on image recognition. The authors also report that the teacher discovers novel curricula and guides the student to better performance than training it alone. The evidence supports adaptive teaching in the studied prediction tasks, with the teacher learning how to respond to the student during training.
icml-2020-student-teacher-curriculum-lea.tldr: A reinforcement-learning teacher selects training batches based on a student's weights, learning curricula that improve performance in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many stochastic gradient descent iterations are needed to make gradients small when optimizing a smooth function. A small gradient indicates approximate stationarity, which is a useful target even when a function is nonconvex. The analysis focuses on gradient norms rather than treating every notion of optimization success as interchangeable.

The authors provide results showing that the classical O(epsilon to the power minus four) upper bound for making the average gradient norm smaller than epsilon cannot generally be improved without a combination of additional assumptions. This obstacle persists even when attention is restricted to convex quadratic functions. Thus, simply choosing that familiar function class does not remove the stated worst-case difficulty.

For nonconvex functions, the paper also finds that whether SGD can minimize gradients is highly sensitive to the chosen optimality criterion. This makes the precise definition of success consequential when comparing guarantees. The results identify limits on improving SGD's iteration complexity and explain why stronger conclusions require careful attention to both assumptions and the quantity being controlled.
icml-2020-the-complexity-of-finding-stat.tldr: SGD's classical gradient-norm complexity cannot generally improve without combined additional assumptions, even for convex quadratics.

paragraphs: Linear neural networks offer a setting for studying training dynamics, but their optimization landscapes still contain non-strict saddle points. This paper identifies conditions under which gradient flow provably trains such networks despite those obstacles. It also analyzes training complexity, addressing both whether training succeeds and the computational demands associated with that success.

The authors develop machinery for identifying the stable set of gradient flow and use it to strengthen earlier linear-network results. They describe their findings as apparently the first to move beyond the lazy-training regime that has dominated much neural-network theory. This is a claim about the reach of the analysis, with the authors' qualification about priority preserved.

A central assumption is that the network contains a layer with one neuron. This includes networks with a scalar output, but does not cover all linear architectures. Extending the theory to every linear network remains an open problem. Within the stated scope, the work provides convergence and complexity results that account for training behavior beyond the previously emphasized regime.
icml-2020-training-linear-neural-network.tldr: The paper establishes gradient-flow convergence and complexity results beyond lazy training for linear networks containing a one-neuron layer.
